did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with three invitations to praise: to sing joyfully, shout aloud, and acknowledge the Lord as “the Rock of our salvation”—the source of stability and deliverance.
Thanksgiving in the chapter is expressed aloud and through song: “Let us come before him with thanksgiving” and “with music.” This describes worship as a shared and celebratory act.
The Lord’s greatness is also presented in terms of his kingship: he is described as “the great King,” and his supremacy extends over all the powers referred to here as “gods.”
The verse places the depths of the earth alongside the mountain peaks to emphasize that all the world’s regions are in the Lord’s hands.

The sea and the dry land are described as belonging to the Lord: the sea is his handiwork, and the dry land was formed by his hands. Thus, the chapter presents the Lord as both owner and Creator of nature.
The sequence of verbs—“let us bow down,” “let us kneel,” and “let us bow low”—emphasizes humility, submission, and honor before the Lord, our Maker.
The people are portrayed through two images of belonging and closeness: “the people of his pasture” and “the flock under his care.” Immediately afterward comes a call to listen to his voice “today.”
The warning “Do not harden your hearts” recalls “Meribah” and “Massah in the wilderness,” teaching that hardening one’s heart is presented as the opposite of listening to the Lord’s voice.

The wilderness generation is described as testing and trying the Lord, even though they had seen his works. The chapter thus emphasizes that witnessing miracles does not replace faith, listening, and faithfulness.
The forty years of wandering are connected in the chapter with a criticism of a generation described as “a people whose hearts went astray”—a generation that did not know the Lord’s ways.
The chapter ends with an oath that they would not enter “my rest.” The phrase describes a place of rest that the rebellious generation would not be allowed to enter.
